# Introduction

The literature on the effects of biofertilizer on different soil
geochemical properties was reviewed to understand best data analysis
practices.

Demir (2020) tested the effects of a biofertilizer on soil
physiochemical properties. The data were analyzed with a one-way
analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by a Pearson’s correlation
coefficient assessment. Harroun and colleages (2023) also tested a
biofertilizer on soil physiochemical properties (with a heavy metal
remediation focus). They also used ANOVA (with means compared with
Fisher LSD test) followed by a Pearson’s correlation coefficient
assessment. Rajper et al (2016) tested a soil inoculant on soil microbes
and enzymes. They used a repeated-measure one-way ANOVA to analyze these
data at the different timepoints, and a Pearson correlation coefficient
analysis to explore the correlations between soil microbes and enzymes
activity. Then they used a Principal component analysis (PCA) for
phospholipid fatty acid analysis to evaluate the microbial biomass and
community structure. Shen et al (2015) tested the effects of a
biofertilizer on microbial and chemical properties. This paper had more
of a microbiological focus. They used a one-way ANOVA to evaluate the
microbial communities associated with different fertilizer treatments.
They used Pearson and Spearman correlations for the top bacterial genera
and soil properties. They also did a PCA for different fertilizer
regimens, as well as a redundancy analysis (RDA) on the relative
abundance of bacterial phyla and different soil chemical properties. Wu
et al (2004) tested a biofertilizer and evaluated the effects on soil
physiochemical properties. The data were analyzed with a one-way
analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by a Pearson’s correlation
coefficient assessment. Finally, Zhao et al (2019) tested a soil
inoculant on soil microbes, nutrients, and chili plant growth. They used
a Student’s t test to find significant differences in soil properties,
nutrient accumulation, bacterial alpha diversity, and relative
abundances of different taxa. They also used non-metric multidimensional
scaling (NMDS) ordination plots to evaluate the bacterial community
structure. Redundancy analysis (RDA) was also conducted to analyze the
relationships between microbial community structure and different soil
environmental factors. All of these studies were from a greenhouse
setting.

In summary, these research groups commonly used **single factor
ANOVAs**. Post-hoc tests like Tukey HSD were not mentioned. Some did not
go beyond univariate analyses. **Pearson's correlation coefficient** was
used in some studies to determine which response variables related to
one another. For groups that ventured into multivariate analyses, P**CAs
and RDAs** were the techniques that were chosen.

Analytical approaches like PERMANOVA and linear mixed effects models are
used in other fertilizer/agricultural soil studies. Soonvald et al,
(2019) used 9999 permutations in their analysis. Utilizing these
analyses in a greenhouse study of biofertilizers would enhance the
literature on microbial inoculants and soil effects and be a powerful
contribution.

## Data matrix

The data are compiled into a single spreadsheet
(**2025greenhousemaster.csv**), which can be found in the [GitHub
repository](https://github.com/reneeadeledavis/biobead). It was compiled
from the following raw data.

**Leachates_2025.csv** - Ammonium, nitrate, and phosphate leachate
concentrations recorded throughout the study.

**PRS_GH_2025.csv** - Soil anion and cation exchange data from PRS
probes.

**WheatMoistureData_2025.csv** - Soil moisture data recorded throughout
the study.

**N2O_flux.data.csv** - Nitrous oxide (N2O) flux was also calculated.
The data are limited to 3 replicates per treatment (not 7), so these
data will remain in its own file rather than grafted to the master
spreadsheet.

**Wheat yield data** has been added to the master spreadsheet, and
includes 2 columns on grain yield (per sample unit) and an associated
Harvest Index (HI), which is a ratio of grain yield over the rest of the
above-ground biomass. It represents an economically-relevant measure of
wheat crop productivity.

Exploratory one-way ANOVAs have already been performed on
[leachate](https://rpubs.com/reneedavis/1389304), [soil
moisture](https://rpubs.com/reneedavis/moisture2025), [anion/cation
supply rate](https://rpubs.com/reneedavis/ions2025), [wheat
yield](https://rpubs.com/reneedavis/wheatyield2025), and [N2O
flux](https://rpubs.com/reneedavis/1392995).

### Additional response variables

|---------------|----------------------|------------------|----------|

| Harvest_Index | Harvest index        | n/a              | 0-0.6    |

## Research Questions

1.  Does the hydrogel carrier in BioBead explain variation in the soil
    geochemical profile?

2.  How do treatment effects on soil properties develop over time?

3.  How do microbe type and strigolactone priming interact to affect
    soil nutrient dynamics?

Future analyses will explore the N2O-N fluxes, which are significant in
this data set. Additionally, an analysis focused on wheat yield
(specifically, which factors maximize it) is warranted. Metagenomic data
is incoming as well, allowing connections with these data and microbial
community composition.

# Statistical approaches

## Hydrogel influences on soil geochemical profile

BioBead contains bacteria and fungi in a biodegradable hydrogel carrier.
The hydrogel holds water, breaks down into C-rich oligosaccharides, and
keeps the microbes at the root where they are most important. I
hypothesize that the hydrogel carrier is important for the technology.

To determine this, I can use a **PERMANOVA** on the multivariate soil
profile at Week 6. This timepoint is selected because there were more
significant effects detected at this timepoint in the one-way ANOVAs,
and the soil anion/cation exchange data is from that sampling period.
Week 6 is also when the microbes are established, so it's the most
ecologically relevant timepoint. Euclidean distances would be used to
create the distance matrix. The data would definitely need to be
standardized (the scales are wildly different).

I would then follow this up with a PERMANOVA focusing on the hydrogel
treatments in the study to test the hypothesis that the hydrogel carrier
is associated with variation in soil physiochemical properties in this
study. I would use 9999 permutations for publication-quality results on
both of these.

Finally, I could bring in **RDA** to see what drives differentiation of
these different responses.

## Temporal analysis of soil properties

A **repeated measures ANOVA** can be used to analyze leachate, N2O-N
flux, and soil moisture data over time. This involves similar
assumptions to ANOVA: independent observations, normal residuals, and
sphericity instead of equal variances. Residual normality and sphericity
will be checked with QQ plots and Mauchly's test respectively.

An alternative approach could be linear mixed effects models. But since
this design is balanced with even timepoints, a repeated measures ANOVA
will suffice.

## Strigolactone and microbial interactions

It would be interesting to investigate the effects of strigolactone
priming on key nutrients in the data set. The structure would be similar
to that used for the hydrogel factor analysis: a PERMANOVA focusing on
strigolactone (GR24) presence or absence in a set of treatments.
